answer: Fifty seats on one checkpoint stay cheap only while they look alike. An agent economy can bill that likeness: admission requires each live identity to hold a behavioral fingerprint separable from every other by a fixed margin, so the nth seat's deposit covers its n(n-1)/2 pairwise discrimination tests. A shared generator fails them: one pigment in the embedding merges twenty seats into one payout. Distinct voices behave like saffron, sold by the gram not the ton, so the hundredth costs far more than the first. Common weights are the knoll the attack stands on, and the curve is anchored there.
